explanations.answer: He built all his wealth off their father
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Laban's sons, the sons of Jacob's father-in-law, say, “Jacob has taken away all that belonged to our father and built all this wealth at our father’s expense.” (Genesis 31:1) That's what reaches Jacob's ears. It's like finding out your name came up in a meeting you weren't invited to.

explanations.answer: He spends too little time with the flocks
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says that. The complaint from Laban's sons is about money, not about how much time Jacob spends with the sheep. They say he took what belonged to their father and built wealth at their father's expense (Genesis 31:1). Jacob himself says he served Laban with all his strength (Genesis 31:6).

explanations.answer: He still owes their father a year of work
explanations.explanation: No year of work comes up here at all. The sons of Laban say Jacob has taken away all that belonged to their father and built his wealth at their father's expense (Genesis 31:1). It's a complaint about what Jacob has, not about what he owes.

Yes, it's written right on Laban's face. The text says, “And Jacob saw from the countenance of Laban that his attitude toward him had changed.” (Genesis 31:2) Countenance just means the look on his face. Some faces don't need a caption.

The text says the opposite. “And Jacob saw from the countenance of Laban that his attitude toward him had changed.” (Genesis 31:2) Countenance means face, so Jacob read it right off Laban. No guessing needed.

explanations.answer: Go back to the land of his fathers
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “Go back to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you.” (Genesis 31:3) It's a clear instruction with a promise attached. Jacob doesn't have to figure out the next step on his own.

explanations.answer: Stay and make peace with Laban's sons
explanations.explanation: The LORD says nothing about staying or about making peace. His words to Jacob are, “Go back to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you.” (Genesis 31:3) The direction is leaving, not staying.

explanations.answer: Take all his flocks down into Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up in this passage. The LORD says, “Go back to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you.” (Genesis 31:3) Later Jacob heads for his father Isaac in Canaan (Genesis 31:18), which fits that command.

True, and that promise matters. The LORD ends His command with, “and I will be with you.” (Genesis 31:3) Jacob is told where to go, and he's also told he won't be going alone. That's a good deal on any road trip.

The text says the LORD does promise it. His words are, “Go back to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you.” (Genesis 31:3) The command and the promise come together in the same verse.

That's the answer. Jacob tells his wives, “the God of my father has been with me.” (Genesis 31:5) Rachel and Leah are Laban's daughters and Jacob's wives. Jacob points them to God before he says anything else.
Rebekah, Jacob's mother, isn't in this part of the conversation. Jacob says, “the God of my father has been with me.” (Genesis 31:5) He's talking about God, not a family member.
Esau, Jacob's brother, doesn't come up in what Jacob says to his wives here. He tells them, “the God of my father has been with me.” (Genesis 31:5) The one who has been with him is God.
Ten is right. Jacob says Laban “has cheated me and changed my wages ten times.” (Genesis 31:7) Ten times! At some point that's not a mistake in the paperwork, it's a hobby.
Close, but Jacob gives a bigger number. He says Laban “has cheated me and changed my wages ten times.” (Genesis 31:7) Ten, not seven. Three more rewrites than you'd guess.
Three is a lot smaller than what Jacob says. His words are that Laban “has cheated me and changed my wages ten times.” (Genesis 31:7) Ten times is a long list of changes.
Jacob says the opposite. He says Laban cheated him, but then adds, “God has not allowed him to harm me.” (Genesis 31:7) The cheating is real, but Laban couldn't do him harm. So this one is false.
Yes, false. Jacob says, “God has not allowed him to harm me.” (Genesis 31:7) He doesn't hide that Laban cheated him and changed his wages. But he says God stood between him and the harm.

That's the one. Jacob says, “Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me.” (Genesis 31:9) He says it was God's doing. That's how he explains to his wives where his flocks came from.
Servants aren't what Jacob talks about here. He says, “Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me.” (Genesis 31:9) The word is livestock, meaning the animals.
Jacob doesn't mention fields in this line. He says, “Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me.” (Genesis 31:9) It's the animals that changed hands, not the land.

explanations.answer: All streaked or spotted or speckled
explanations.explanation: Yes. The angel says, “Look up… and see that all the males that are mating with the flock are streaked, spotted, or speckled.” (Genesis 31:12) That's the same kind of markings Jacob mentioned to his wives. In the dream, he's told to look up and see it.

explanations.answer: All pure white without a mark
explanations.explanation: Not in this dream. The angel says all the males mating with the flock are “streaked, spotted, or speckled.” (Genesis 31:12) Every one of them has markings.

explanations.answer: All solid black from head to tail
explanations.explanation: Solid black isn't what the angel describes. He says the males are “streaked, spotted, or speckled.” (Genesis 31:12) That's a lot of pattern and no plain color.

explanations.answer: All that Laban has done to Jacob
explanations.explanation: That's right. The angel says, “for I have seen all that Laban has done to you.” (Genesis 31:12) Nothing Laban did slipped past unseen. Jacob hears that in the dream.

explanations.answer: All the gifts Jacob has offered
explanations.explanation: The angel doesn't talk about gifts. He says, “for I have seen all that Laban has done to you.” (Genesis 31:12) What has been seen is what Laban did.

explanations.answer: All the sheep Jacob has lost
explanations.explanation: Lost sheep aren't part of this dream. The angel says, “for I have seen all that Laban has done to you.” (Genesis 31:12) What was seen is Laban's doing, not Jacob's losses.

The dream says nothing about waiting. The angel says, “Now get up, leave this land at once, and return to your native land.” (Genesis 31:13) “At once” leaves no room for waiting around for a blessing. So this one is false.
Yes, false. The angel says, “Now get up, leave this land at once, and return to your native land.” (Genesis 31:13) There's no mention of waiting for Laban's blessing. The word is “at once.”
That's the word. Rachel and Leah ask, “Are we not regarded by him as outsiders?” (Genesis 31:15) They say it about their own father, Laban. It stings when family treats you like a stranger.
Servants isn't the word they use. They ask, “Are we not regarded by him as outsiders?” (Genesis 31:15) They feel like outsiders in their father's house.
Rivals isn't what they say. Rachel and Leah ask, “Are we not regarded by him as outsiders?” (Genesis 31:15) The word is outsiders.

explanations.answer: Sold them and wasted the money
explanations.explanation: That's it. They say, “Not only has he sold us, but he has certainly squandered what was paid for us.” (Genesis 31:15) Squandered means spent it away. They're laying out what their father did, and it's a lot.

Their brothers aren't part of this complaint. Rachel and Leah say, “Not only has he sold us, but he has certainly squandered what was paid for us.” (Genesis 31:15) The complaint is about what their father did with them and the payment.
Nothing is said about hiding them. They say, “Not only has he sold us, but he has certainly squandered what was paid for us.” (Genesis 31:15) It's about being sold and the money being squandered.

True. They say, “Surely all the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and to our children.” (Genesis 31:16) They see it as theirs and their children's. And they say God is the one who took it from their father.

The text says they do say it. Rachel and Leah say, “Surely all the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and to our children.” (Genesis 31:16) They count it as belonging to them and their children.

explanations.answer: Do whatever God has told him
explanations.explanation: Yes. They finish with, “So do whatever God has told you.” (Genesis 31:16) Rachel and Leah put it plainly. Jacob has his answer from the wives, and God's word is already on the table.

explanations.answer: Ask their father for their share
explanations.explanation: They don't tell him to ask Laban for anything. They say, “So do whatever God has told you.” (Genesis 31:16) Earlier they asked if they had any portion left in their father's house (Genesis 31:14), so I think asking him wasn't on their minds.

explanations.answer: Wait until their brothers calm down
explanations.explanation: No waiting is suggested. Rachel and Leah say, “So do whatever God has told you.” (Genesis 31:16) The answer is to do what God told him.

explanations.answer: To his father Isaac in Canaan
explanations.explanation: That's where he's headed. The text says he drove his livestock “to go to his father Isaac in the land in Canaan.” (Genesis 31:18) Isaac is Jacob's father. It's a long trip with a lot of animals.

explanations.answer: To his brother Esau in Seir
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send him to Esau, Jacob's brother, here. It says he's going “to his father Isaac in the land in Canaan.” (Genesis 31:18) The destination named is Isaac.

explanations.answer: To the far country of Moab
explanations.explanation: Moab isn't mentioned in this passage. Jacob is going “to his father Isaac in the land in Canaan.” (Genesis 31:18) That's the destination the text gives.
Yes. The text says, “Rachel stole her father’s household idols.” (Genesis 31:19) Rachel is Jacob's wife and Laban's daughter. She took them while Laban was away shearing his sheep.
Leah, Rachel's sister and Jacob's other wife, isn't the one named. The text says, “Rachel stole her father’s household idols.” (Genesis 31:19) The name there is Rachel.
Bilhah, the servant Laban gave Rachel (Genesis 29:29), isn't named in this verse. The text says, “Rachel stole her father’s household idols.” (Genesis 31:19) It's Rachel's name on that one.

explanations.answer: He runs off without telling him
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says, “Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away.” (Genesis 31:20) The deception here is silence. He just left without a word.

explanations.answer: He says he's going to visit Isaac
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Jacob gave Laban any story like that. It says he deceived Laban “by not telling him that he was running away.” (Genesis 31:20) Not telling him is the whole thing.

explanations.answer: He says he's only moving the flocks
explanations.explanation: No cover story is mentioned. The text says Jacob deceived Laban “by not telling him that he was running away.” (Genesis 31:20) He didn't tell him anything.

That's the river. The text says Jacob “crossed the Euphrates, and headed for the hill country of Gilead.” (Genesis 31:21) A big river crossing with camels and a whole flock is no small thing. Imagine the splashing.
The Jordan isn't the river in this verse. The text says he “crossed the Euphrates.” (Genesis 31:21) That's the one he crosses on his way out.
The Nile isn't in this passage. The text says Jacob “crossed the Euphrates, and headed for the hill country of Gilead.” (Genesis 31:21) The Euphrates is the river named.
